t.1.29.1: Sūta said: Having become as if made of Jāmbūnada gold, blazing with spreading rays, the bird forcibly entered, as the rush of waters enters the ocean.
t.1.29.2: Near the amṛta he saw an iron wheel, its rim edged with razors and its blades sharp, whirling about without ceasing.
t.1.29.3: He saw that machine, well fashioned by the gods, exceedingly terrible in form, dreadful, radiant like blazing fire and the sun, a cutter-down of those who would steal the soma.
t.1.29.4: As soon as he saw an opening in it, the sky-goer turned about, and, contracting his body in an instant, he flew in through the space between the spokes.
t.1.29.5: And there, beneath the wheel, were two exceedingly dreadful ones, radiant as blazing fire, with tongues like lightning, with blazing mouths and blazing eyes.
t.1.29.6: He saw two excellent serpents, venomous of eye, of great might, ever wrathful and swift, stationed there for the very purpose of guarding the amṛta.
t.1.29.8: Suparṇa swiftly covered the eyes of the two with dust, and, his form unseen, he drove them on from every side.
t.1.29.7: The two had eyes ever blazing with fury and ever unblinking; whomever even one of them looked upon would swiftly be reduced to ashes.
t.1.29.9: Treading upon the bodies of those two, Vainateya, the sky-goer, swiftly cut them through the middle, and then he rushed toward the soma.
t.1.29.10: Then the mighty Vainateya, tearing up that amṛta and smashing the contrivance, flew up swiftly, full of valor.
t.1.29.11: Without drinking the amṛta, the mighty bird swiftly seized it, and the sky-goer flew off unwearied, veiling the radiance of the sun.
t.1.29.13: The imperishable god said to the sky-roamer, "I am a giver of boons." He who travels through the sky chose: "May I stand above you."
t.1.29.12: Then Vainateya met with Viṣṇu in that sky, and Nārāyaṇa was pleased with him for that deed done without greed.
t.1.29.14: And he spoke these words once more to Nārāyaṇa: "May I be free from old age and death even without the amṛta."
t.1.29.15: Having accepted those two boons, Garuḍa said to Viṣṇu: "I too give a boon to you; let the Blessed Lord also choose one."
t.1.29.17: But Indra, flying after the bird, struck him on the body with his thunderbolt, that sky-goer, the enemy of the gods, who was carrying off the amṛta by force.
t.1.29.16: Kṛṣṇa chose him, the mighty Garutmant, as his mount, and the Blessed Lord made him his banner, saying to him, “You shall stand above.”
t.1.29.18: Then Garuḍa, best of birds, struck thus by the thunderbolt in the fray, laughed and spoke to Indra in a gentle voice.
t.1.29.19: I shall honor the seer from whose bone the thunderbolt was born; and I shall honor the thunderbolt too, and you as well, O Śatakratu.
t.1.29.20: Here I cast off a single feather, whose end you will never find; for never is there any pain for me from the striking of the thunderbolt.
t.1.29.21: Then all the creatures there, filled with wonder, said of him, beholding his beautiful plumage, "Let this one be Suparṇa, the Fair-Feathered!"
t.1.29.23: I wish to know your strength, which is supreme and unsurpassed, and I desire an endless friendship with you, O best of birds.
t.1.29.22: And seeing that marvel, the thousand-eyed Puraṃdara thought, “This bird is a mighty being,” and addressed him.
